movements.summary: An encampment-based protest against economic inequality and the political power of finance, organised without formal leadership or a list of demands, which put the distributional question into mainstream political language.
keyFacts: The occupation of Zuccotti Park in New York began on 17 September 2011 following a call from Adbusters.
'We are the 99%' became its organising slogan, drawing on research into top-1% income concentration.
It used general assemblies and consensus process, and declined to issue demands — a deliberate choice that was also its most criticised one.
It spread to hundreds of cities worldwide in autumn 2011.
Zuccotti Park was cleared on 15 November 2011.
Offshoots included Occupy Sandy's disaster relief and the Rolling Jubilee debt-buying project.
criticisms: The refusal to formulate demands is widely argued to have prevented any legislative outcome.
Consensus process proved slow and vulnerable to disruption at scale.
Encampments faced real problems of safety and sanitation.
Defenders argue it permanently changed the vocabulary of inequality in American politics, which no bill had managed.
movements.sources: Contemporary reporting; Adbusters call (July 2011); academic retrospectives.

movements.name: The American Indian Movement
movements.summary: An Indigenous rights organisation founded in Minneapolis in 1968, which combined urban community patrols and services with high-visibility occupations asserting treaty rights and sovereignty.
keyFacts: Founded in 1968, initially around police accountability and services for Native people in Minneapolis.
The occupation of Alcatraz (1969–71), by Indians of All Tribes, cited an 1868 treaty provision on surplus federal land.
The Trail of Broken Treaties march in 1972 ended in the occupation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs building in Washington.
The occupation of Wounded Knee in 1973 lasted 71 days and involved sustained exchanges of fire with federal forces.
Leonard Peltier was convicted over the 1975 deaths of two FBI agents at Pine Ridge; the case has been contested ever since.
It contributed to the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975) and the American Indian Religious Freedom Act (1978).
criticisms: Internal violence and the unresolved killing of Anna Mae Aquash in 1975 remain a serious charge against it.
Some tribal governments viewed it as urban activists speaking over elected leadership.
Confrontation drew heavy federal surveillance and prosecution that fractured the organisation.
Defenders point to the legislation and the lasting shift in how treaty rights are argued.
movements.sources: National Archives; Britannica; contemporary reporting; Indian Self-Determination Act (1975).

movements.name: Rastafari as political movement
movements.summary: A movement originating among the Jamaican poor in the 1930s which fused Ethiopianism, Garveyite self-reliance and biblical interpretation into a critique of colonial society — 'Babylon' — and a politics of repatriation and African dignity.
keyFacts: It emerged after the 1930 coronation of Haile Selassie I in Ethiopia, read by early adherents as prophetic fulfilment.
Marcus Garvey's teaching of African pride and self-reliance is its central political antecedent.
'Babylon' names the colonial and commercial order; livity and ital practice are its everyday discipline.
The Coral Gardens incident of 1963 in Jamaica involved serious state violence against adherents.
Haile Selassie's 1966 visit to Jamaica drew enormous crowds; a 1955 Ethiopian land grant at Shashamane supported repatriation.
Reggae — Bob Marley above all — carried its political vocabulary worldwide from the 1970s.
criticisms: Adherents were criminalised and institutionalised in Jamaica for decades.
Patriarchal norms around the role of women have been criticised within and outside the movement.
Haile Selassie's own record as a ruler is at odds with his status in the movement.
Commercial reggae is argued to have detached the symbols from the politics.
movements.sources: Jamaican national archives; Coral Gardens apology (2017); academic literature on Rastafari.

movements.name: The Arab uprisings
movements.summary: A wave of mass protests across North Africa and the Middle East demanding dignity, employment and the end of entrenched authoritarian rule, with sharply divergent outcomes by country.
keyFacts: Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation in Sidi Bouzid on 17 December 2010 triggered the Tunisian uprising.
Ben Ali left Tunisia in January 2011; Mubarak resigned in February 2011 after the occupation of Tahrir Square.
'Bread, freedom, social justice' was the central Egyptian slogan — economic as much as political.
Tunisia produced a new constitution in 2014 and the National Dialogue Quartet received the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize; the democratic settlement was substantially reversed from 2021.
Libya, Syria and Yemen descended into civil wars with foreign intervention; Egypt returned to military rule in 2013.
Bahrain's protests were suppressed with Gulf Cooperation Council military assistance.
criticisms: Absence of organised parties and programmes left movements unable to hold power once regimes fell.
Western intervention in Libya is widely argued to have produced state collapse.
The outcomes have been used to argue that uprisings without institutions make matters worse.
Defenders note the underlying grievances were real, remain unaddressed, and have produced further waves since.
movements.sources: Contemporary reporting; Nobel Peace Prize 2015 citation; academic retrospectives.

maxims.term: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains
maxims.attribution: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract (1762)
maxims.gloss: Opening line framing the problem of legitimate authority: how can the freedom people are born with be reconciled with the constraints society imposes?

maxims.term: Property is theft!
maxims.attribution: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, What Is Property? (1840)
maxims.gloss: A provocation, not a call to abolish all possession: Proudhon attacked property-as-domination (rent, interest, exploitation of others' labor), while defending personal possession.

maxims.term: The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it
maxims.attribution: Karl Marx, Theses on Feuerbach (1845; pub. 1888)
maxims.gloss: The rallying line of praxis: theory is judged by whether it transforms conditions, not merely explains them.

maxims.term: From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs
maxims.attribution: Popularized by Karl Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875); phrase used earlier by Louis Blanc
maxims.gloss: A distributive ideal of higher-stage communism: contribution by capacity, distribution by need.

maxims.term: That government is best which governs least
maxims.attribution: Motto quoted by Henry David Thoreau, 'Civil Disobedience' (1849)
maxims.gloss: A touchstone of limited-government and libertarian thought (Thoreau attributes it as a saying, then pushes it further).

maxims.term: The personal is political
maxims.attribution: Second-wave feminism; associated with Carol Hanisch's 1969 essay (title added by editors)
maxims.gloss: Private-seeming matters (housework, sexuality, family) reflect and reproduce public power relations, and are therefore political.

maxims.term: War is the continuation of politics by other means
maxims.attribution: Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832, posthumous)
maxims.gloss: War is not a breakdown of policy but an instrument of it — an extension of political aims by force.

maxims.term: The end justifies the means
maxims.attribution: A summary often (loosely) attributed to Machiavelli's The Prince (1532)
maxims.gloss: The consequentialist claim that outcomes can validate the methods used — frequently invoked in, and criticized within, political ethics; Machiavelli's actual text is subtler.

maxims.term: Liberté, égalité, fraternité
maxims.attribution: Motto of the French Revolution / French Republic
maxims.gloss: 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' — three ideals whose tensions (liberty vs. equality especially) organize much of modern political debate.

maxims.term: Who says organization, says oligarchy
maxims.attribution: Robert Michels, 'iron law of oligarchy', Political Parties (1911)
maxims.gloss: Michels argued that even democratic organizations tend to develop a ruling few — a standing challenge to theories of mass democracy.

maxims.term: The tyranny of the majority
maxims.attribution: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835/1840); developed by J. S. Mill
maxims.gloss: Democracy can oppress minorities and dissenters through sheer numbers and social conformity, not only through government — hence constitutional limits on majority power.

maxims.term: The price of liberty is eternal vigilance
maxims.attribution: Commonly attributed to Jefferson; no such sentence appears in his writings
maxims.gloss: The nearest documented source is John Philpot Curran (1790) on the condition of liberty. A maxim whose attribution is itself a lesson in citation.

maxims.term: Man is by nature a political animal
maxims.attribution: Aristotle, Politics I.2
maxims.gloss: Zōon politikon — a creature of the polis. The claim is that political life completes human nature rather than constraining it.

maxims.term: The life of man, solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short
maxims.attribution: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651
maxims.gloss: Describes the state of nature without a common power, and so grounds the argument for sovereignty.

maxims.term: Government of the people, by the people, for the people
maxims.attribution: Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address, 1863
maxims.gloss: The formulation echoes Wycliffe's Bible preface and Daniel Webster; Lincoln made it the standard definition of democratic legitimacy.

maxims.term: All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others
maxims.attribution: George Orwell, Animal Farm, 1945
maxims.gloss: The commandment as finally revised — a compressed account of how revolutionary equality is undone from within.

maxims.term: The best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market
maxims.attribution: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., dissenting in Abrams v. United States, 1919
maxims.gloss: The origin of the 'marketplace of ideas'. Holmes had voted the other way in Schenck the same year, which is part of the story.

maxims.term: Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants
maxims.attribution: Louis Brandeis, Other People's Money, 1914
maxims.gloss: The founding sentence of disclosure-based regulation; usually paraphrased as 'sunlight is the best disinfectant.'

maxims.term: Taxation is the price we pay for a civilized society
maxims.attribution: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., paraphrased from Compañía General de Tabacos v. Collector, 1927
maxims.gloss: The actual words were 'Taxes are what we pay for civilized society.'

maxims.term: A rising tide lifts all boats
maxims.attribution: New England Council slogan, popularised by John F. Kennedy
maxims.gloss: The standard shorthand for growth-first economics, and the standard target of distributional critiques of it.

maxims.term: Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither
maxims.attribution: Benjamin Franklin, Pennsylvania Assembly reply to the Governor, 1755
maxims.gloss: Written about a tax dispute with the Penn family, not about national security — the context is almost always dropped.

maxims.term: The state is the great fiction by which everybody seeks to live at the expense of everybody else
maxims.attribution: Frédéric Bastiat, The State, 1848
maxims.gloss: The classical-liberal account of public spending as mutual plunder.

maxims.term: The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice
maxims.attribution: Martin Luther King Jr., paraphrasing Theodore Parker (1853)
maxims.gloss: Parker's original is longer and more cautious: he could not finish the curve by sight, and divined it by conscience.

maxims.term: Freedom is never voluntarily given by the oppressor; it must be demanded by the oppressed
maxims.attribution: Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail, 1963
maxims.gloss: The letter's answer to clergymen who urged patience — the fullest statement of the case for direct action.

maxims.term: Ubuntu — I am because we are
maxims.attribution: Southern African philosophical tradition; 'umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu'
maxims.gloss: A person is a person through other persons. Invoked in South Africa's transition as the ground of restorative rather than retributive justice.

maxims.term: The Mandate of Heaven
maxims.attribution: Classical Chinese political doctrine (Zhou dynasty onward)
maxims.gloss: Tianming: rule is held on condition of virtue and can be withdrawn — which makes rebellion against a failed ruler legitimate rather than treasonous.

maxims.term: Matsya-nyaya — the law of the fish
maxims.attribution: Classical Indian political literature, including the Arthaśāstra and the Mahabharata
maxims.gloss: Without governance the big fish eat the small. The classical Indian justification for the state, parallel in function to Hobbes's state of nature.

maxims.term: Who guards the guardians?
maxims.attribution: Quis custodiet ipsos custodes? — Juvenal, Satires VI
maxims.gloss: Written about guarding a wife, borrowed by political theory as the problem of accountability at the top of any hierarchy.
